newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Hungary assures investors on energy price rises.
newsitem.headline: Hungary assures investors on energy price rises.

text.p: Hungary's new industry and trade minister said on Monday that energy price rises in the pipeline would assure Western investors in the country's energy sector of the eight-percent profit margin the government promised them.

"Once the real costs have been established, the eight percent return on invested assets will be granted to investors," Szabolcs Fazakas told Reuters in an interview. "That's what the government promised and we are very keen on keeping our word."

The government is expected later this week to discuss recommendations by a government commissioner, Imre Karl, on the amount by which energy suppliers should be allowed to put up energy prices on January 1.

Western utilities such as German giant RWE and the French EdF paid more than two billion forints ($12.65 million) for large stakes in Hungary's energy distribution companies at the end of 1995 and were promised an eight-percent return on investment from January 1997.
An appendix to the original contracts recommended staggered rises in March and October 1995 to prepare for market-based rates in January.

However, the government in August put off the October rise until January and appointed Karl to review the energy prcing policy after the Hungarian Energy Office, following consultations with the utilities, recommended a reported 39 percent October rise.
The postponement provoked fears among investors that the January rise would not be high enough to generate the promised returns.
According to press reports on Monday, Karl will recommend an average rises of around 22 percent, well below those proposed earlier by the Energy Office.

Fazakas declined to confirm any figure but said that once Karl had submitted his proposals negotiations with owners would continue to establish a common basis for calculating the eight per cent margin built into the price rise.

"The differences will arise around what you calculate the eight per cent from," he said. "If you take out factors like insurance, maintenance, the efficiency of the company and so on then you come to another figure."

Fazakas was appointed to the industry and trade portfolio at the end of last month to replace Tamas Suchman who resigned following disclosures of millions of dollars in consultancy fees paid to an adviser to the state privatisation agency APV, which at the time came under Suchman's control.
The whole executive board of APV was also dismissed.
Fazakas said foreign investors should note the way the government acted if they were worried about endemic corruption.

"The government acted quickly and decisively, it was a purifying fire," he said. "I think it was a very important time for those for those who didn't know how far to go to realise that their possibilities are limited," he said. ($1=158.93 Forint)
